analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 15 or more workers to provide at least seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2007 with 24 Democratic and independent cosponsors, it was referred to the Senate health committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Families Act would have required every employer with 15 or more employees to give full-time workers at least seven paid sick days a year, and part-time workers a prorated share, to use when they are sick, for medical appointments, or to care for a sick child, spouse, parent, or family-like caregiver relationship. Workers could not be fired or penalized for using the leave, and the Labor Department would enforce the rules. Nearly half of American workers at the time had no paid sick leave at all, including about 79 percent of families in the lowest-earning quartile. The bill was introduced in March 2007 by Senator Edward Kennedy with 24 cosponsors and never received any committee action or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the gainers would have been the roughly half of American workers who then had no paid sick leave — disproportionately low-wage workers in retail, restaurants, child care, and other service jobs, and the women who carry most family caretaking duties. A full-time worker would have gotten seven paid days a year to recover from illness, see a doctor, or stay home with a sick child without losing pay or their job. Family members they care for would have benefited too, since sick workers who cannot stay home spread illness through workplaces, schools, and child care, and early treatment catches disease before it becomes an expensive emergency.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers without paid sick leave

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers with 15 or more employees to provide at least seven paid sick days a year for full-time workers, and a prorated amount for those working 20-30 hours a week, usable for their own illness, injury, or preventive care, or to care for a child, parent, spouse, or a person who stands in a family-like relationship to them [S2] [S3].

Lets workers use the time for routine and preventive medical appointments, not just emergencies, and requires that foreseeable appointments be scheduled in a way that limits disruption to the employer [S3].

Protects workers from being fired, demoted, or marked down for taking the leave, prohibits counting sick leave against 'no-fault' attendance policies, and gives workers the right to sue for lost wages plus damages, with attorney's fees paid by a violating employer; the Department of Labor also gets investigative and enforcement powers [S2] [S3].

Bars employers from eliminating, reducing, or redesignating paid leave they already provide in order to comply, and lets employers with existing policies that already meet the standard keep them unchanged [S3].

The bill's findings state that nearly half of American workers lacked paid sick leave at the time, including 79 percent of families in the lowest-earning quartile, and that sick workers who cannot stay home spread illness in workplaces, schools, and child care [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on employers with 15 or more employees, who would pay wages for up to seven days a year not worked, manage scheduling around leave, keep compliance records, and face Labor Department enforcement and private lawsuits for violations. Businesses in low-margin sectors with many hourly workers — restaurants, retail, hotels — would have felt it most. Employers who already offered comparable paid leave would have owed nothing new.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a real cost to employers: they must pay wages for up to seven days a year not worked, absorb scheduling disruptions, and keep compliance records under Department of Labor oversight, with costs falling hardest on low-margin businesses like restaurants, retail, and hotels that employ many workers who currently lack paid sick leave [S2] [S3].

The bill's definition of family is open-ended: leave may be used to care for 'any individual related by blood or affinity whose close association with the employee is the equivalent of a family relationship,' which leaves employers with uncertainty about who qualifies and invites disputes [S3].

Some workers are left out: employers with fewer than 15 employees, and employees working fewer than 20 hours a week or fewer than 1,000 hours a year, get nothing under the bill, so the lowest-hours workers, who are also among the least likely to have paid leave, remain uncovered [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were broad and concrete: before this bill, nearly half of American workers had no paid time off when they or a family member were sick, and among the lowest-earning quartile that figure was 79 percent [S3]. Seven paid days is a modest floor, and the bill took several steps to keep it manageable for employers: it applies only to businesses with 15 or more workers, lets employers count existing paid-leave policies that already meet the standard toward compliance, bars them from cutting leave they already provide to comply, caps carryover at seven days, lets employers require a doctor's note only for absences longer than three days, and gives them eighteen months' notice before it applies to union contracts [S2] [S3]. The real costs are the wages paid for days not worked, the greatest for employers in low-margin industries that employ many of the very workers who currently lack sick leave, plus compliance and recordkeeping burdens. On the other side of the ledger, the bill's own findings cite evidence that presenteeism costs employers roughly $180 billion a year in lost productivity, and that early, routine care reduces emergency care and public health costs [S3]. The main design weakness is the open-ended definition of who can be cared for — "any individual related by blood or affinity whose close association ... is the equivalent of a family relationship" — which gives employers little certainty about how far the obligation runs [S3]. On balance the bill traded a modest, bounded employer cost for guaranteed paid sick time for the tens of millions of workers who had none.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read, and sent to the Senate's health and labor committee, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress expired.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 15, 2007 by Senator Kennedy with introductory remarks published in the Congressional Record, and was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5] [S1].

The complete action history contains only three entries — introduction, sponsor remarks, and committee referral — with no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no roll call at any point during the two-year Congress [S5] [S1].
It ended the Congress with 24 cosponsors in addition to its sponsor, all Democrats or allied independents [S4] [S1].

The bill's findings section laid out the case: nearly half of American workers lacked paid sick leave, 79 percent of the lowest-earning families lacked it, and sick workers forced to work spread disease in workplaces, schools, and child care [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have borne the cost of providing paid sick days, particularly in retail, restaurants, and hospitality, are better off because the bill never moved; workers without paid sick leave gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have borne the cost

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 15, 2007 and delivered introductory remarks in the Senate [S5] [S1] [S3].

for.name: 24 Senate cosponsors (22 Democrats, 2 allied independents)
for.role: Senate cosponsors, including Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden, and Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the bill text lists all of them jointly introducing it on March 15, 2007 [S3] [S4] [S1].

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied business groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal paid-sick-leave mandates as an employer cost, lobbying against similar proposals; no opposition to this specific bill appears in the congressional record because it never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or allied independent; no Senate Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call breakdown exists.

industries.industry: Employers of low-wage service workers (restaurants, retail, hotels, and other businesses with 15 or more employees)
industries.note: The bill obliges these employers to pay for up to seven days of leave a year per full-time worker, a cost concentrated in low-margin industries that employ many of the roughly half of American workers who then had no paid sick leave. They would also carry new recordkeeping and enforcement exposure under Department of Labor oversight [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Employers that already provide seven or more paid sick days
industries.note: These employers keep their existing policies unchanged if the policies meet the bill's requirements, and are barred from cutting them to comply, so most larger and white-collar employers face little direct cost [S3].

More workers attending routine and preventive appointments means more billable primary care, while the bill's findings argue early care would reduce emergency room use and overall medical costs paid by insurers and businesses [S3].
